title: Booker T. Washington on the Efficacy Belief
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart uses two lines from Booker T. Washington's Up from Slavery to argue that how a student defines success is one of the most powerful levers on their Efficacy belief. He contrasts a growth-oriented definition of success, measured by obstacles overcome rather than rank achieved, with an externalized, comparative definition (being valedictorian, getting an A) that he says is nearly guaranteed to produce feelings of failure for almost everyone who adopts it. He illustrates the danger with his own ninth-grade students who set out to be class valedictorian, noting only one of roughly two hundred can hold that title, and says he actively counsels students away from that framing every year. His practical alternative is teaching students to use the language of growth toward mastery as the daily objective, which he says allows students at every level of preparation to feel a legitimate sense of Efficacy. The piece previews Define Success, Early and Often, one of the ten strategies in his forthcoming book Will to Learn.
points: Locates the source of Washington's resilience in his definition of success as the obstacles which he has overcome, not the position reached — a definitional move Stuart argues teachers can replicate with students.
Warns that externalized, comparative success metrics like valedictorian status or class rank mathematically guarantee failure for the vast majority of students who adopt them.
Offers growth toward mastery as a specific daily-use phrase that reframes success as accessible to students at every current skill level, not just top performers.
Positions success as a subjective construct teachers actively shape through language, not a fixed external target, with real consequences for which students can feel Efficacy.
quotes: I have begun everything with the idea that I could succeed, and I never had much patience with the multitudes of people who are always ready to explain why one cannot succeed.
I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
How you or I or our students define success is perhaps the most important factor in helping or hindering their Efficacy belief.

On the other hand, when success is defined externalistically, perfectionistically, or comparatively — e.g., I need to be the top person in the class, I need to get an A on the test — then it is very likely that you actually cannot succeed.

For example, when some of my ninth grade students set out to be valedictorians of their class, the odds are not in their favor. Only one out of the two hundred or so that they graduate with can have this title.
It's so much better to focus on growth toward mastery. When success is conceived of this way, students of all levels of academic preparation can feel a sense of Efficacy in school.
